title: Change of basis, similarity, and diagonalization
terms: coordinate vector; change-of-basis matrix; similar matrices; diagonalizable operator; algebraic multiplicity; geometric multiplicity.

A matrix is diagonalizable over its field exactly when it has a basis of eigenvectors. An eigen-
value’s geometric multiplicity is its eigenspace dimension; its algebraic multiplicity is its mul-
tiplicity in the characteristic polynomial. Their equality for every eigenvalue, together with
splitting of that polynomial, characterizes diagonalizability. Distinct eigenvalues suffice, but are
not necessary. A repeated root by itself does not prove failure.
The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree satisfying m(A) = 0. Since

solution.text:
The first basis vector is a 2-eigenvector and the second is a 3-eigenvector: T(1, 1) = (3, 3).
The columns in the new coordinates are therefore (2, 0) and (0, 3).

question.text:
A real 4 × 4 matrix A satisfies (A − I)(A − 2I) = 0 and tr A = 6. What is det A?
(A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 8 (E) 16

solution.text:
The annihilating polynomial has distinct roots, so A is diagonalizable with eigenvalues in
{1, 2}. If k eigenvalues equal 2, its trace is 4 + k = 6, hence k = 2. The determinant is
2 2
1 · 2 = 4.

The images of the basis vectors are (2, 3) and (2, −3). Their coordinates in this basis
are (5/2, −1/2) and (−1/2, 5/2), respectively. These coordinate columns form the stated
matrix.

A real 5 × 5 matrix A has characteristic polynomial (t − 1) (t − 2) and rank(A − I) = 3. Which
conclusion must hold?
(A) A is diagonalizable because it has real eigenvalues.
(B) The eigenspace for eigenvalue one has dimension three.
(C) A is not diagonalizable because the eigenspace for eigenvalue one has dimension two.
(D) A has a nonreal eigenvalue.
(E) A is singular.

solution.text:
Rank–nullity gives dim ker(A − I) = 5 − 3 = 2, while the algebraic multiplicity of one is three.
This shortfall prevents an eigenbasis, regardless of the eigenspace dimension for two. The
3 2
determinant is 1 2 = 4, so singularity is not the issue.

question.text:
Which pair of real matrices cannot be similar?
(A) Two matrices with different coordinate representations of the same linear map
(B) Two matrices with different orthonormal eigenbases
(C) Two matrices with different entries
(D) Two matrices with different eigenvectors
(E) Two matrices with different minimal polynomials

solution.text:
Similarity preserves polynomial identities and hence the minimal polynomial. Entries,
eigenvectors, and coordinate bases can change under similarity. Different coordinate matri-
ces of the same operator are precisely related by a basis-change similarity.
